content.title: About
content.content: Alfalfa sprouts are the young shoots of alfalfa seeds (Medicago sativa) grown in controlled conditions without chemical fertilizers. They have a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. Raw sprouts are commonly used in salads, smoothies, sandwiches, and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Alfalfa sprouts are rich in vitamins K, C, and B-complex.
They contain more than 40 % protein by weight, making them one of the most protein‑dense vegetables.
Alfalfa has long been used as livestock feed, but its sprouts are popular in human health foods.
Sprouts can be ready in just 3–5 days after soaking the seeds.
Raw alfalfa sprouts are a staple in many Asian dishes such as rolls and soups.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Sprouts provide vitamin K (important for blood clotting), vitamin C (antioxidant) and B‑vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Approximately 40 % of their dry weight is plant protein, which helps tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: They contain calcium, iron, magnesium and phosphorus, essential for bone health and metabolic functions.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber in sprouts promotes intestinal motility and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup of raw alfalfa sprouts provides about 25 kcal, making them an excellent addition to calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Raw sprouts can harbor Salmonella or E. coli; purchase from reputable sources and rinse thoroughly before use.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to alfalfa, experiencing skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: Because of their delicate texture, sprouts can pose a choking risk for children under 3 years old.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add alfalfa sprouts to fresh salads, smoothies, sandwiches, rolls, and soups. They can also be used as a garnish. If desired, briefly blanch them in hot water to reduce microbial load.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sprouts in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. They stay fresh for 3–5 days. Discard any wilted or slimy portions before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean beef, boiled rice and vegetables (carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens). It is served with a smooth gravy that ties the ingredients together and adds a savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is an excellent source of iron, zinc and vitamin B12.
Rice provides complex carbohydrates that give lasting satiety.
Broccoli is rich in vitamin C and glucosinolates, compounds with anti‑cancer properties.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale) contain high amounts of vitamin K and folate.
Gravy is often made from broth and a small amount of flour, giving it a thick, aromatic consistency.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: Beef protein helps build and repair muscle tissue.

items.title: Provides steady energy
items.content: Complex carbs from rice supply a stable glucose release.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Vitamin C from broccoli and leafy greens helps neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium from leafy greens contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Zinc from beef and vitamin A from carrots boost immune function.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Consuming large amounts of beef may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Prepared gravy often contains salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: If the gravy is thickened with wheat flour, it should be avoided by those with celiac disease.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Beef must be cooked thoroughly to eliminate the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot. Garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or soy sauce to taste. Vegetables can be eaten as whole pieces or mashed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared meal in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For freezing, pack in portion‑size bags and use within 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Breadsticks are soft wheat‑based sticks topped with grated Parmesan cheese. They belong to the fast‑food/restaurant category and are commonly served as an appetizer or side dish for soups and salads. The dough is made from flour, water, yeast, and a small amount of butter, then the sticks are sprinkled with Parmesan and baked quickly until golden.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Parmesan gives the breadsticks a distinctive nutty aroma and enhances their flavor.
Originally served in Italian eateries, they have become popular worldwide because of their simplicity and versatility.
The soft texture is achieved by a short baking time and the addition of butter to the dough.
Breadsticks are often used as a vehicle for dipping sauces such as marinara, cheese, or garlic aioli.
Adding herbs like rosemary or oregano together with Parmesan creates an even more aromatic version.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Parmesan provides about 35 g of protein per 100 g, helping to support muscle maintenance.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Hard cheese is rich in calcium and phosphorus, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑leavened dough supplies B1, B2, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: When whole‑grain flour is used, breadsticks become a source of soluble and insoluble fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: Unlike sweet snacks, breadsticks typically contain no added sugar, making them a more balanced option.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Parmesan can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy allergies or lactose intolerance.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Grated Parmesan is often salty; people monitoring sodium intake should limit portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of butter in the dough and cheese topping, breadsticks are relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional wheat dough contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve breadsticks hot, dipped in marinara, ranch, garlic yogurt, or enjoy them plain as a snack. They are easy to break into bite‑size pieces for sharing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep breadsticks in an airtight container at room temperature for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate them—they stay soft for up to a week. Reheat briefly in the oven (5‑7 min) before serving to restore a slight crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Peach cobbler is a classic American dessert made of sweet peach filling topped with a biscuit‑like crust. The filling usually consists of fresh or canned peaches mixed with sugar, lemon juice, and spices such as cinnamon and nutmeg, while the topping is a simple dough of flour, butter, sugar, and milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cobbler originated in the 19th‑century Southern United States, where peaches were abundant.
Traditional cobbler is baked in a ceramic dish, which helps the topping become golden and crisp.
Peaches are rich in vitamin C and beta‑carotene, giving them their bright orange hue.
There are many cobbler variations: blueberry, apple, apricot, and even pumpkin.
The original recipe calls for the dough to be dropped in coarse spoonfuls rather than fully covering the fruit.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Peaches provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in peaches aids digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in peaches protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Healthy fats in the topping
items.content: Butter in the crust supplies monounsaturated fats that can be heart‑friendly in moderation.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Peaches contain potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Cobbler often contains a lot of added sugar, which can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Butter allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy should use plant‑based butter substitutes.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The crust and sugar make cobbler calorie‑rich, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Gluten presence
items.content: Traditional dough uses wheat flour, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve warm peach cobbler often with a scoop of vanilla ice cream or a dollop of whipped cream. It can be enjoyed as a dessert after a meal or as a sweet snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven before serving to restore the crisp topping.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanuts, dry roasted, salted are whole peanuts that have been roasted without added oil and lightly salted. The dry‑roasting process gives them a crunchy texture and a rich, nutty aroma, while a touch of salt enhances the flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts.
Dry roasting without oil preserves more nutrients compared with oil‑fried peanuts.
Salt is usually added after roasting to keep the nuts crisp.
Peanuts are a staple in many world cuisines, from Asian sauces to African stews and American snacks.
Dry roasted peanuts are the base for peanut butter, confectionery, and trail mixes.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Peanuts provide about 25 % protein, making them a valuable plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Healthy monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats
items.content: These fats support heart health and help absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peanuts contain niacin, thiamine, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: magnesium, phosphorus, potassium
items.content: These minerals aid muscle function, nerve signaling, and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Resveratrol and other phenolic compounds in peanuts help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are one of the most common food allergens and can cause severe reactions.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because they are energy‑dense, portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The salted version may be unsuitable for people with hypertension or kidney disease.

items.title: Aflatoxins
items.content: Improper storage can allow mold growth that produces aflatoxins, so proper storage conditions are essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dry roasted salted peanuts are perfect as a snack on their own, tossed into salads, added to Asian dishes, mixed into granola or trail‑mixes, or used as a crunchy topping for soups and desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life store in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.
